Cauchy's Integral Formula [S+N]¶

The deepest single result of complex analysis. If $f$ is holomorphic on an open set containing a closed disc $\overline{D_R(z_0)}$, then for any $z$ in the interior

$$f(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{|\zeta - z_0| = R} \frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta - z}\,d\zeta.$$

In words: values of a holomorphic function inside a disc are determined by its values on the boundary. That's a wildly more rigid property than smooth real functions have — $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has no analogous boundary-value control.

Three consequences land immediately:

  1. Holomorphic ⇒ infinitely differentiable. Differentiate the integrand under the integral sign.
  2. Holomorphic ⇒ analytic. The function equals its Taylor series locally.
  3. Maximum modulus principle. $|f|$ on a domain attains its max on the boundary.

This notebook walks the formula and these consequences.

Verifying the formula numerically [S+N]¶

Take $f(z) = z^2 + 1$ (entire) and $z_0 = 0$, $R = 1$. The formula at $z = 0.3 + 0.4i$ predicts $f(0.3 + 0.4i) = (0.3 + 0.4i)^2 + 1$.

In [26]:
f_eval(z) := z^2 + 1$
z_check : 0.3 + 0.4 * %i$
truth_val : expand(f_eval(z_check))$
print("f(0.3 + 0.4i) =", truth_val, "  (=", float(realpart(truth_val)),
      "+", float(imagpart(truth_val)), "i)")$

/* Approximate the contour integral on |ζ| = 1 numerically */
N_pts : 2000$
dt : 2 * float(%pi) / N_pts$
total : 0 + 0*%i$
for k : 0 thru N_pts - 1 do block([t, zeta, num, den],
  t : k * dt,
  zeta : exp(%i * t),
  num : f_eval(zeta) * %i * exp(%i * t),
  den : zeta - z_check,
  total : total + num / den * dt)$
formula_val : total / (2 * float(%pi) * %i)$
print("Cauchy formula prediction:", formula_val)$

f(0.3 + 0.4i) = 0.24*%i+0.9299999999999999   (= 0.9299999999999999 + 0.24 i)

Cauchy's formula for derivatives¶

Differentiate under the integral sign:

$$f^{(n)}(z) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i} \oint \frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta - z)^{n+1}}\,d\zeta.$$

In particular, all derivatives exist as soon as one does. For $f(z) = z^2 + 1$ at $z = 0$, $f''(0) = 2$. Verify:

In [27]:
/* Numerical: f''(0) = 2! / (2πi) ∮ f(ζ)/ζ³ dζ */
total2 : 0 + 0*%i$
for k : 0 thru N_pts - 1 do block([t, zeta, num, den],
  t : k * dt,
  zeta : exp(%i * t),
  num : f_eval(zeta) * %i * exp(%i * t),
  den : zeta^3,
  total2 : total2 + num / den * dt)$
fpp_val : 2.0 * total2 / (2 * float(%pi) * %i)$
print("f''(0) via Cauchy formula:", fpp_val)$
print("(true f''(0) = 2)")$

Bounds: the Cauchy estimate¶

If $|f| \le M$ on $|\zeta - z_0| = R$, then

$$|f^{(n)}(z_0)| \le \frac{n!\,M}{R^n}.$$

This is the ML inequality applied to the formula for derivatives.

Liouville's theorem falls out: a bounded entire function ($f$ holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$, $|f| \le M$ globally) has $|f^{(n)}(z_0)| \le n!\,M / R^n$ for arbitrarily large $R$, so $f^{(n)}(z_0) = 0$ for all $n \ge 1$. Thus $f$ is constant.

Fundamental theorem of algebra is a one-line corollary: if $p(z)$ is a non-constant polynomial with no zeros, $1/p$ would be entire and bounded — by Liouville, constant. Contradiction.

Maximum modulus principle¶

If $f$ is holomorphic on a connected open set $\Omega$ and $|f|$ has a local maximum in $\Omega$, then $f$ is constant. Equivalently: on a bounded domain, $|f|$ attains its maximum on the boundary.

Geometrically: a holomorphic function can't have an interior peak in $|f|$ unless it's flat. This is a consequence of Cauchy's integral formula too — average of $f$ around a small circle equals the centre value, which forces no interior local max.

Demonstrate by sampling $|f(z)|$ for $f(z) = z^2 + 1$ on a disc:

In [28]:
ax_draw3d(
  explicit(cabs((x + y*%i)^2 + 1), x, -1, 1, y, -1, 1),
  title="|z² + 1| on the unit disc — maxes on the boundary",
  xlabel="Re z", ylabel="Im z", zlabel="|f(z)|",
  colorscale="Viridis"
)$

The maxima of $|z^2 + 1|$ over the closed unit disc both sit on the boundary circle (at $z = \pm 1$, where $|f| = 2$). The interior is strictly lower.

Why the boundary determines the interior¶

This is the deepest difference from real analysis. A real $C^\infty$ function on $[a, b]$ is not determined by its boundary values $f(a)$, $f(b)$ — there are infinitely many smooth functions with any chosen pair. A holomorphic function on a disc is determined by boundary values via Cauchy's formula.

Equivalently: holomorphic functions have far less freedom than real smooth ones. They're solutions of a $\bar\partial$-PDE, which is severely restrictive.

Putting it together¶

We've covered:

  • Holomorphic = complex differentiable in all directions ⇔ Cauchy-Riemann.
  • Holomorphic on a simply connected domain ⇒ contour integrals are zero (Cauchy's theorem).
  • Cauchy's integral formula reads off interior values from the boundary.
  • ⇒ holomorphic ⇒ $C^\infty$ ⇒ analytic.
  • ⇒ maximum modulus, Liouville, FTA.

The next notebook tackles isolated singularities: poles, residues, and the residue theorem — the toolkit that unlocks classical real-integral evaluations.

Reference¶
